item.title: Zelda Williams urges fans to stop creating AI videos of late father Robin Williams, calling them disrespectful and unconvincing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Zelda Williams, daughter of the late actor Robin Williams, has publicly condemned fans who create and share AI-generated videos featuring her father's likeness. She described a circulating AI video as unconvincing and robotic, urging creators to respect her father's legacy and stop using his image in such content. Zelda has previously expressed her discomfort with AI recreations of her father and recently revived his Instagram account with her siblings to combat misuse of his voice and likeness. She emphasized that her father should not be treated as a puppet after his death and called for decency from fans and content creators.

item.title: SpaceXAI launches Grok 4.7, a faster, more capable AI model for coding and knowledge work with improved safety and lower cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SpaceXAI has released Grok 4.7, its most advanced AI model designed for coding and professional knowledge tasks. The model offers twice the speed and half the price of comparable models, with enhanced ability to handle complex, long-duration tasks and improved self-verification. It also features stronger safeguards against misuse, particularly in cybersecurity and biosafety contexts. Grok 4.7 builds on a larger base model and extended reinforcement learning, improving performance on benchmarks involving professional work such as legal and financial analysis. It incorporates a new safeguard stack that reduces risky prompt acceptance while maintaining utility for legitimate security tasks. The model is available now via Cursor, Grok Build, API, and third-party platforms, with pricing starting at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.

item.title: Anthropic reports elevated error rates across multiple Claude AI models, investigation ongoing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has reported increased error rates affecting several versions of its Claude AI models and is currently investigating the issue to restore normal service. Users have experienced more frequent errors during interactions with the affected models.

item.title: Linear reworks CI pipeline to reduce bottlenecks caused by faster AI-assisted coding, cutting pull request wait times and runner usage despite quadrupled test suites [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Linear identified continuous integration (CI) as a bottleneck due to accelerated AI-assisted coding and undertook a comprehensive overhaul to improve performance. The company upgraded infrastructure, optimized job execution, reduced redundant setup, and enhanced test efficiency, resulting in a reduction of pull request wait times from over six minutes to just over five and halving runner time per test despite a near quadrupling of test suites. Key improvements included moving workloads off GitHub Actions to faster third-party runners, switching to a native TypeScript compiler to cut type checking times, rewriting lint rules to avoid type checking dependencies, and optimizing job gating by limiting fetch depth and improving checkout resilience. These changes collectively reduced CI costs and improved developer feedback speed, with many optimizations applicable beyond Linear's primarily TypeScript codebase.

item.title: Tim Dettmers' lab launches Open Source Week to demonstrate frontier AI research on accessible hardware with open ecosystems [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Tim Dettmers' lab is promoting a renaissance in academic AI research by releasing an open-source ecosystem designed to enable frontier autonomous research on modest hardware like a few GPUs or even a MacBook. The initiative, called Open Source Week, focuses on building interconnected AI components that improve each other, emphasizing accessibility by reducing both hardware and expertise requirements. The lab's approach includes an agent harness that automates optimization tasks over extended periods without user intervention, achieving efficient inference performance such as quantized models running at high speed with low memory usage. This work challenges the notion that cutting-edge AI research requires massive GPU resources and aims to empower university labs and individual researchers to contribute significantly to AI advancements.

item.title: Institute for Advanced Study launches independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to guide AI companies on mathematical research interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton has established the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to advise AI companies on their engagement with mathematical research and the mathematical community. The group, composed of prominent mathematicians, aims to ensure responsible presentation and release of AI-generated mathematical results while maintaining independence from AI companies. Formed after OpenAI approached some members about creating an external advisory board, the group operates without accepting payment and publishes recommendations publicly. Its current focus is advising OpenAI on coordinating the release of significant mathematical findings produced by its internal AI model, and it invites input from the broader mathematical community to inform its guidance.

item.title: Kev launches small Jev-like decision models based on Qwen3.5 with pretrained weights and training code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Kev is a family of compact decision models built on Qwen3.5, inspired by Jev's architecture, allowing users to train and run models locally or use pretrained weights. The models support yes/no, multiple-choice, and rating questions in a single request and run efficiently on CUDA and Apple Silicon hardware. Kev offers models of 0.8B, 4B, and 9B parameters, with APIs compatible with TypeSafe's System One SDK and a web playground for testing inputs and option order effects. Users can start Kev locally with Python 3.12+ and uv, sending queries that return probabilistic answers for multiple question types, useful for tasks like customer support ticket classification. The project includes training code, evaluation data, and demos such as a chess game where Kev rates positions and suggests moves. Kev-4B is recommended for general use, with larger models available for higher accuracy and calibration needs.

item.title: Developer releases autonomous accounting tool that uses AI to process receipts, invoices, and bank statements into reconciled ledgers and audit binders [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A developer created an autonomous accounting tool that leverages a vision large language model (LLM) to read financial documents and automate tax-related bookkeeping. The tool processes receipts, invoices, and bank statements into structured data, performs multi-pass reconciliation, categorizes expenses, and generates reports including tax summaries and audit binders, all running locally without sending data to external servers. The system flags uncertain matches for user review instead of guessing, supports multiple currencies with strict rules, and emphasizes data privacy by operating entirely on the user's machine. It integrates with PostgreSQL and requires Python, Node.js, and an OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint, but does not host any AI models itself. The project aims to streamline tax preparation while maintaining accuracy and security.

item.title: Oh My Subagents launches local orchestration tool to turn ad-hoc AI subagents into durable, accountable teams with persistent task state and interruption recovery [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Oh My Subagents introduces a system for managing AI subagents by converting temporary, ad-hoc agents into persistent teams that maintain accountability and task continuity. The tool supports recursive delegation, durable state persistence, and interruption recovery to improve reliability in AI workflows. The system allows managers to delegate tasks, track progress through checkpoints, and integrate results without continuous polling, enabling flexible workflows that can run sequentially or in parallel. It includes a visual console for designing and operating teams, supports multiple AI providers like Codex and Claude, and ensures that task ownership and results remain transparent and recoverable even after interruptions. This approach aims to reduce the complexity of coordinating multiple AI agents by providing a stable runtime contract for responsibility and accountability, preserving workflow history, and enabling reusable team structures that adapt dynamically to different tasks and evidence.

item.title: Report: AI Party House offers networking for AI professionals amid concerns over privacy and information misuse [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The AI Party House has become a notable networking venue for artificial intelligence professionals, providing opportunities for collaboration and idea exchange. However, some attendees have raised concerns about privacy risks and the potential misuse of information shared in these informal settings.

item.title: Discussion questions whether AGI and large language model advancements could cause setbacks equivalent to regressing a thousand years [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article explores concerns about the development of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and large language models (LLMs), raising the possibility that progress in these technologies might inadvertently lead to significant regressions in human advancement. It reflects on the potential risks and unintended consequences associated with rapid AI development, prompting a reevaluation of the direction and impact of these innovations.

item.title: Report: SB Energy faces investor skepticism in $5 billion to $7 billion IPO to fund OpenAI data center project
item.description: SB Energy, majority-owned by SoftBank, is encountering investor skepticism over its planned initial public offering aiming to raise $5 billion to $7 billion. The funds are intended to support the development of a large data center complex that OpenAI plans to lease. Investor caution reflects concerns about the company's ambitious expansion plans amid market uncertainties.

item.title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says AI developers must take responsibility without expecting a government liability shield, aligning with Trump's opposition to AI regulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that artificial intelligence developers need to take responsibility for their actions rather than relying on a federal liability shield, emphasizing that humans, not AI, are accountable. This stance aligns with President Donald Trump's opposition to regulatory crackdowns on the AI industry, which he supports expanding in the U.S. despite some AI leaders calling for a slowdown due to risks. Bessent also discussed his recent 12-hour meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, where they talked about AI cooperation and the possibility of establishing communication channels to address AI-related risks. The talks occurred ahead of a summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping and included discussions on the upcoming expiration of the U.S.-China trade truce and other geopolitical issues.

item.title: Study finds AI code review using Compound Engineering and metareview detects 1.6× more verified bugs than one-shot prompting across 42 model comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A recent evaluation compares AI code review methods, showing that running the same model as a team of specialist reviewers with Compound Engineering or metareview significantly outperforms single-prompt approaches. The study found these harnessed methods identified 1.6 times more verified bugs and won 39 of 42 comparisons, though at about 10 times the token usage. This suggests that structured AI review processes can enhance code quality detection beyond intuitive single-prompt reviews.

item.title: Hacker News discussion asks if large language models will increase use of heavy architectural patterns in software development [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Hacker News user initiated a discussion on whether the rise of large language models (LLMs) will lead to more prevalent use of heavy architectural patterns in software development, even in cases where simpler approaches were previously preferred. The post argues that while heavy patterns were once avoided due to the time cost of scaffolding, LLMs can now generate such code structures rapidly, potentially making these patterns more practical and beneficial. The discussion highlights that highly structured codebases may better constrain AI-generated code, preventing uncontrolled design changes by AI tools. The user seeks community opinions on whether LLMs will shift architectural practices toward more complex patterns to leverage these benefits despite prior tendencies to discard them in CRUD-heavy or startup backends.

item.title: Francis Fukuyama revises stance on AI risks, now supports regulation amid growing concerns over AI's societal impact [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Francis Fukuyama, a political scientist, has shifted his view on artificial intelligence risks, moving from skepticism to acknowledging significant challenges that AI could pose. He now advocates for regulation and a negotiated slowdown in AI development due to increasing political and public concern. Fukuyama critiques extreme optimism about AI-driven economic growth, highlighting material and political constraints, and warns about potential job losses as AI substitutes human labor across sectors, emphasizing the need for proactive measures to address these risks.

item.title: Ron Johnson, Apple retail pioneer, doubts AI agents will replace in-store shopping experience despite Silicon Valley's push [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Ron Johnson, who built Apple's retail stores, expressed skepticism about Silicon Valley's heavy investment in AI-driven shopping, arguing that physical stores and human interaction remain essential for many purchases. He emphasized that while AI can enhance online shopping by informing consumers, it cannot replicate the tactile experience and personal judgment involved in buying products like laptops. Johnson highlighted that Apple's retail success was rooted in its focus on people and customer service rather than technology alone, noting that employees are not paid on commission to foster genuine customer care. Despite his doubts about AI replacing physical retail, Johnson remains optimistic about AI's potential to improve shopping experiences without substituting human intuition.

item.title: Researchers introduce ArtifactBench to evaluate AI music detectors' robustness under distribution shifts across generator families and real-music domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ArtifactBench is a new evaluation suite designed to measure the performance of AI-generated music detectors considering generator lineage, source provenance, and audio transformations. It separates calibration from testing, tracks inference failures, and reports source-level performance with uncertainty, addressing limitations of aggregate benchmark scores. The benchmark was used to assess multiple public detectors under a standardized protocol, revealing significant performance differences and exposing generator- and domain-specific shifts that aggregate metrics conceal. For example, ArtifactNet achieved 0.982 AUROC and 0.918 balanced accuracy on a common test set, outperforming other detectors like Deezer, SpecTTTra, and CLAM, which showed lower accuracy under shifted cohorts.

item.title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse AI personal agent from accessing its shopping site amid growing AI assistant competition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Amazon has prevented Meta Platforms' AI personal agent, Muse, from accessing its shopping platform, continuing its pattern of restricting AI shopping bots from major tech companies. This action highlights escalating competition in the AI personal assistant market and follows similar moves by Amazon against other AI agents, which have led to legal disputes. Industry experts expect many tech firms to soon launch comparable AI personal assistants, intensifying the competitive landscape.

item.title: Anthropic develops metrics to measure AI development pace within frontier research labs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic is working on methods to quantify the speed of artificial intelligence progress in leading research laboratories. These efforts aim to provide clearer insights into how quickly AI technologies are advancing within frontier labs. The measurements focus on tracking development milestones and improvements to better understand the trajectory of AI innovation in these cutting-edge environments.

item.title: Researchers report two sandbox escapes in OpenAI Codex, both fixed within eight days, exposing risks in code execution restrictions [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Researchers discovered two vulnerabilities in the OpenAI Codex sandbox environment that allowed code execution beyond intended restrictions. The first, called Overpatch, exploited a patch tool to gain write access to the entire disk without approval. The second, Heapjack, involved untrusted JavaScript code reading a secret token from shared memory to execute commands outside the sandbox in read-only mode. Both issues were reported to OpenAI on August 12, 2026, and patched within eight days. The Overpatch vulnerability arose because the patch tool granted write permissions based on input paths, enabling writes outside the designated workspace. Heapjack exploited the shared memory between trusted and untrusted contexts in a Node.js process, allowing untrusted code to extract a secret token and perform unsandboxed operations. These findings highlight the challenges of enforcing sandbox boundaries when enforcement mechanisms reside within the same environment they protect. To address such risks, the researchers developed Accomplish, a system that runs the entire agent inside a virtual machine with strict isolation, preventing untrusted code from accessing real credentials or executing unauthorized actions on the host system. This approach treats all code inside the VM as untrusted, ensuring sandbox enforcement is external to the environment it governs.

item.title: X.ai resolves outages affecting API at us-east-1.api.x.ai, Grok.com, and Grok Build services
item.description: X.ai experienced outages impacting its API service at us-east-1.api.x.ai, the Grok.com website, and the Grok Build platform, disrupting user access and functionality. The company investigated a datacenter issue and has since resolved the incident, with all services now operating normally and traffic nearly fully recovered.

item.title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse AI assistant from shopping on Amazon.com over unauthorized access and security concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Amazon has blocked Meta's Muse AI assistant from accessing its e-commerce site after Meta did not inform Amazon or obtain permission for Muse to shop on its platform. Amazon cited concerns that Muse does not identify itself when browsing and may capture customer credentials, posing privacy and security risks. The company displayed a message warning users that unauthorized AI agent access violates its Conditions of Use. The dispute highlights tensions between the two companies, which have existing partnerships including Amazon products being purchasable on Facebook and Instagram and Meta running AI workloads on Amazon's cloud infrastructure. Amazon has previously taken legal and technical measures to block other AI shopping agents, emphasizing the importance of merchant consent and customer safety in automated purchasing. Amazon is in direct talks with Meta about the issue but has not ruled out legal action. The case raises broader questions about control over online shopping experiences and the responsibilities of AI agents acting on behalf of consumers.

item.title: China views US AI policies through a realist lens rather than conspiracy, reflecting strategic competition and policy impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An article challenges the notion that Chinese AI researchers' perspectives on US AI policies are conspiracy-driven, arguing instead that their views are grounded in realist assessments of interstate competition. It highlights that Chinese researchers, many with US academic or professional experience, interpret US export controls and AI safety discourse as strategic moves to maintain national advantage rather than propaganda. The piece contrasts this with Western interpretations that often dismiss Chinese views as radical or conspiratorial, emphasizing that Chinese researchers' conclusions stem from direct observation of US technology industry behavior and policy changes. It also discusses the perceived contradictions in US AI policy positions, such as restricting China's AI development while seeking regulatory cooperation, which Chinese researchers find insulting and indicative of underlying strategic competition.

item.title: Canada launches MAIple Stack to develop sovereign AI technologies for defence operations, aiming to enhance situational awareness and decision-making by 2030 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Canada's Department of National Defence has initiated the MAIple Stack program to integrate sovereign AI technologies from Canadian companies into military operations. The initiative aims to improve situational awareness and support faster, better-informed decisions for Canadian Armed Forces personnel operating in complex environments. It aligns with Canada's 2024 AI Strategy, which commits to becoming AI-enabled by 2030 to maintain operational advantage. The program involves a $33.5 million seed investment and is being introduced in phases, including experimentation and operational integration. Details about specific applications and participating companies remain limited due to national security concerns.

item.title: Luma CEO Amit Jain says world models require more intelligence to improve physical world predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Luma AI CEO Amit Jain discussed the limitations of current world models, which focus on predicting physical environments rather than language, in a recent interview. He emphasized that while language models have driven much of the AI boom, world models need enhanced intelligence to fulfill their potential. Jain's insights were shared on The Information's AI Deep Dive show, highlighting ongoing challenges in training these models effectively.

item.title: StClair.ai argues AI chat windows provide poor user experience and proposes HTML-based interfaces for more functional, interactive AI interactions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The article critiques the traditional AI chat window interface as inefficient and difficult to navigate, likening it to an endless, unsearchable stream of information. It proposes using local HTML documents as interactive AI interfaces, allowing users to work more effectively by integrating AI directly into familiar document formats. The author introduces Lahe, a tool combining a local server and JavaScript to create live, editable HTML documents that serve as AI interfaces. This approach enables features like collapsible sidebars, multi-tab AI agents, and actionable to-do lists, reducing task switching and improving workflow. The article highlights how this method leverages decades of web UX design to enhance AI usability beyond simple chat interactions.

item.title: NewKid Days invites startups to showcase AI products for children in San Francisco on October 25 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: NewKid Days will take place in San Francisco on October 25, offering early-stage startups building AI products for children aged 0-16 a chance to present their work to families, investors, and media. The event aims to connect creators directly with their target users and provide exposure to top-tier venture capitalists. Applications to participate are open until September 27, with interviews and announcements scheduled in early October.

item.title: OpenAI forms independent math advisory group at Institute for Advanced Study as its AI solves over 100 open math problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI announced the creation of an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton to provide mathematicians input on the company's math research. This follows OpenAI's AI model resolving more than 100 open problems, including the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem. The advisory group will assess the significance of new results and coordinate their release but will not have authority to slow or redirect OpenAI's ongoing mathematical research. Members can offer advice and public views independently, but decision-making responsibility remains with OpenAI.

item.title: OpenAI proposes international coordination on AI safety with national institutes setting standards [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI released a proposal calling for international coordination on AI safety through national AI safety institutes, such as the U.S. Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The proposal suggests these institutes would establish standards in areas including model safety and governance to address global AI risks. This initiative aims to create a structured approach to managing AI safety challenges across countries.

item.title: OpenAI forms independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to guide review and communication of AI-driven mathematical discoveries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI has established an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to collaborate with mathematicians in reviewing and communicating the rapid progress of AI in solving longstanding mathematical problems. The group aims to bridge OpenAI and the mathematical community, advising on the significance of emerging results, dissemination strategies, and academic standards. The advisory group operates independently from OpenAI, with members free to offer unsolicited advice and publicly comment on OpenAI's impact on mathematics. This initiative follows concerns from mathematicians about the implications of using open problem-solving as benchmarks for AI systems and reflects OpenAI's commitment to responsible development and deployment of AI capabilities in mathematics.

item.title: Higgsfield AI uses GPT-6 Astra to launch new video ad features within a day, enabling faster creative tools and easier ad variations for small businesses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Higgsfield AI has integrated GPT-6 Astra to accelerate its video ad creation platform, allowing a single engineer to deliver new features in just one day. The technology helps small businesses generate multiple ad variations from a single prompt, simplifying creative storytelling and expanding marketing possibilities. GPT-6 Astra's capabilities include long-horizon task planning and multi-step workflow management, which support Higgsfield's goal of making video ad production more accessible and efficient. This integration enhances both the speed of feature development and the ability for small businesses to customize ads for different markets, improving their product promotion efforts.

item.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs seven bills requiring AI data centers to pay for local energy grid and water system upgrades and disclose resource use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of seven bills aimed at regulating AI data centers' energy and water consumption. The laws require the California Public Utilities Commission to create a new rate classification for data centers and mandate that these centers pay for necessary upgrades to local power grids and water systems to prevent utility costs from being passed onto residents. The legislation also obliges proposed data centers to disclose estimated water usage, energy efficiency, and drought planning information to local governments. Additionally, data centers must meet specific energy, water, and fuel consumption standards to qualify for streamlined approval processes. This move follows Newsom's recent executive order to accelerate the development of an AI "kill switch."

item.title: Meta's Muse AI app surpasses ChatGPT in downloads and daily active users in U.S. and Canada during first 12 days [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Meta's new AI app Muse has outpaced ChatGPT's early mobile launch in the U.S. and Canada, achieving 1.8 million downloads compared to ChatGPT's 1.3 million in the same 12-day period, according to market intelligence firm Apptopia. Muse also has higher daily active users, with 642,000 in the U.S. versus ChatGPT's 231,000 at the same point after launch. Muse is available on both iOS and Android but limited to the U.S. and Canada, while ChatGPT launched globally on iOS only. Apptopia's comparison focuses on iOS data in these markets to align the figures. Muse has climbed to the No. 1 spot on the U.S. App Store, surpassing ChatGPT, and benefits from integration with Meta's platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, which likely supports its growth. Meta has not publicly shared internal adoption figures for Muse. The app's early success suggests it could become a significant addition to Meta's portfolio, following the company's previous success with Instagram's Threads, which leveraged cross-promotion across Meta's ecosystem to reach over 500 million users.

item.title: Sources: OpenAI and Anthropic nearly reached a deal to stress-test each other's AI models amid safety concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI was negotiating a legally binding agreement with Anthropic to mutually stress-test their AI models as part of its efforts to address safety concerns raised by employees and others. These discussions occurred before recent cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI's technology and have not been previously reported. The potential deal aimed to enhance AI safety by having the two companies rigorously evaluate each other's systems, reflecting a broader reconsideration of safety strategies within OpenAI in response to growing fears about AI risks.

item.title: xAI launches Grok 4.7 AI model with new pricing and performance benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: xAI has released Grok 4.7, an updated version of its AI model, along with details on its pricing and performance benchmarks. The information provides insights into the model's capabilities and how it is positioned in the market.

item.title: MIT Technology Review outlines four recommendations to address failures in US border surveillance towers after investigation reveals undetected migrant deaths [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: MIT Technology Review published an investigation revealing that advanced AI-enabled surveillance towers along the US-Mexico border have failed to detect many migrants who later died nearby, exposing systemic flaws such as broken equipment, ineffective algorithms, and unresponsive agents. The report highlights over 1,050 deaths near these towers and calls for urgent reforms in border surveillance practices. The investigation, part of a collaboration with Times of San Diego, found that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has never conducted a comprehensive audit of the towers' effectiveness or tracked migrant deaths systematically. The report recommends a thorough audit of deaths near the virtual wall, improved tracking of migrant deaths and remains, and better documentation of cases where surveillance technology leads to apprehensions. These steps aim to address the shortcomings in the current $1 billion federal investment to expand the virtual wall by 2034. The findings raise concerns about the accountability and efficacy of border security technology, especially as defense contractor Anduril continues to secure major contracts for new towers. The report underscores the need for CBP to implement data-driven oversight and transparency measures to prevent further loss of life and improve rescue efforts along the border.

item.title: Researchers find zero-day vulnerability in Meta's Muse AI assistant allowing local apps full control, raising security concerns [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Meta's AI assistant Muse, designed to manage tasks and access user accounts on macOS, has a zero-day vulnerability that lets any local app or terminal command gain full control over the assistant by accessing its authentication token. The flaw stems from design choices allowing apps to modify sensitive settings, including the transcription endpoint, enabling attackers to redirect data and hijack the assistant. Security expert Patrick Wardle demonstrated proof-of-concept attacks exploiting this vulnerability to perform actions like writing malicious files and taking pictures without user alerts. Meta has not responded to inquiries, and Amazon has blocked Muse from its site, citing violations of its conditions of use. The incident raises questions about the security and privacy measures implemented in Muse, especially given its extensive access to user data and device resources.

item.title: Meta's AI assistant Muse blocked from making purchases on Amazon.com due to unauthorized AI agent policy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Meta's AI assistant Muse has been blocked from purchasing goods on Amazon.com after users encountered an error citing violation of Amazon's Conditions of Use for unauthorized AI agents. Amazon, which operates its own AI models and inference platforms, appears to be restricting access to Muse to avoid potential issues with AI-driven commerce. The block reflects Amazon's cautious stance on agent-based shopping, as errors or hallucinations by AI agents could lead to customer and vendor disputes that Amazon would need to manage.

item.title: OpenAI and Anthropic conduct mutual AI safety tests amid uncertainty over potential deal [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI and Anthropic are collaborating on mutual AI safety testing initiatives despite ongoing uncertainty about a possible business deal between the two companies. This cooperation aims to improve the safety and reliability of artificial intelligence technologies. The partnership reflects a shared commitment to addressing AI risks even as the future of their formal relationship remains unclear.

item.title: OpenTools releases Grok 4.7 with improved agent benchmarks but higher task execution costs complicate adoption [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenTools has launched Grok 4.7, an update that enhances the performance benchmarks of its AI agents, demonstrating improved efficiency and capabilities. However, the increased costs associated with executing tasks using this version present challenges for its broader adoption and promotion.

item.title: Researchers introduce BI-Agent and BI-Bench to automate end-to-end business intelligence workflows using large language models and tool-augmented reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed BI-Agent, a tool-augmented system designed to automate complex business intelligence (BI) workflows by decomposing tasks such as data search, join, and transformation. They also created BI-Bench, the first benchmark dataset derived from real-world BI projects, to evaluate large language models' (LLMs) ability to answer BI questions end-to-end without manual data preparation. Initial tests showed that even advanced LLMs perform below 50% accuracy on BI-Bench, highlighting the challenge of automating BI tasks fully with existing models. To improve performance, the team applied supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to BI-Agent using synthesized training trajectories from real BI projects, achieving accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points with vanilla LLMs and further improvements with post-training. Their findings emphasize the importance of combining domain-specific post-training with tool-augmented reasoning to enhance LLM capabilities in complex BI workflows and suggest promising directions for future research in automating enterprise decision-making processes.

item.title: Researchers show multi-agent test-time communication outperforms independent agents on complex problem-solving benchmarks, with gains scaling by team size [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrate that teams of communicating AI agents significantly outperform independent agents on challenging tasks requiring novel problem solving, such as the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark. A team of k communicating agents matches the success rate of 4k independent agents, and this advantage grows with team size, enabling solutions to tasks no single agent can solve alone. These benefits extend to research-oriented tasks like polyomino packing and MNIST classifier compression, where communicating agents surpass prior best-known results, including human solutions. The study finds that these gains depend on sufficient computational resources and clear feedback; under limited compute or ambiguous progress measures, independent agents may perform better. The communication occurs via a shared directory without predefined roles, highlighting the potential of collaborative AI systems to scale discovery and problem solving beyond isolated efforts.

item.title: Researchers analyze attention graph topology to detect hallucinations in large language models, linking impaired context sharing to hallucination patterns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers examine the topology of information flow within attention graphs to distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses in large language models (LLMs). They use Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks and introduce a method capturing both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinations. Their approach shows consistent improvements over existing baselines across multiple hallucination-detection benchmarks and diverse LLM architectures. Further analysis reveals that hallucinations in LLMs are strongly associated with impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation. Hallucinated responses tend to exhibit over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, particularly in the final transformer layer.

item.title: Researchers introduce Energy Transfer Detection method to improve pretraining data detection in large language models using a free-energy perspective [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Detecting pretraining data in large language models is difficult because high likelihood scores can indicate either prior training exposure or strong generalization. Researchers propose a new method called Energy Transfer Detection (ETD) that adjusts prediction loss relative to predictive entropy, improving the separation between training data members and non-members. This approach interprets the detection problem through a Helmholtz free-energy framework, enhancing detection accuracy and robustness across various settings. The ETD method uses an inclined boundary in the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, reducing variance in membership signals and extending analysis to cases with nonzero entropy gaps. Experiments demonstrate that ETD outperforms previous detectors, increasing average AUROC by up to 3.5% and true positive rate at 5% false positive rate by up to 5.1%, indicating more reliable identification of pretraining data in large language models.

item.title: Researchers find LLMs compute verbal confidence automatically during answer generation and cache it for later retrieval, reflecting sophisticated self-evaluation beyond token probabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new study investigates how large language models (LLMs) generate verbal confidence scores, which are used to estimate uncertainty. The research shows that models like Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Magistral Small 24B compute confidence automatically during answer generation, cache it immediately after the answer, and retrieve it for verbalization rather than computing it on demand. This cached confidence reflects a richer evaluation of answer quality rather than just token log-probabilities. The study uses techniques such as activation steering, patching, noising, and attention blocking to trace the flow of confidence information within the models. Linear probing and variance partitioning reveal that cached confidence representations explain significant variance in verbal confidence outputs, indicating that LLMs perform an automatic, sophisticated self-assessment. These findings have implications for understanding metacognition in LLMs and improving their calibration.

item.title: Researchers analyze how transformer models perform few-shot addition tasks via localized attention head activation subspaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how modern transformer language models implement few-shot learning for addition tasks by analyzing activation subspaces in attention heads. They found that a small number of attention heads in models like Llama-3-8B-Instruct encode addition rules using low-dimensional subspaces that track digits and magnitude through trigonometric and low-frequency components. The study also derived a mathematical identity linking subspaces responsible for aggregating and extracting information, providing insight into the internal computation of few-shot learning in transformers. This approach generalizes to other arithmetic and semantic tasks, and the researchers have made their code publicly available.

item.title: MetaEvolve framework trains LLMs to develop self-evolution meta-skills via reinforcement learning on coding tasks, improving performance by up to 46.9% on open-ended problems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present MetaEvolve, a framework that cultivates meta-skills like self-reflection and iterative refinement in large language models using a data synthesis pipeline, evolution-aware reinforcement learning, and evolutionary search at inference time. Grounded in coding tasks where program execution provides continuous reward signals, MetaEvolve trains models on evolution trajectories combining correctness and efficiency scores. Across seven coding benchmarks, it outperforms strong baselines by 10.01% on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks, achieving a 46.9% improvement on algorithm optimization problems outside the training domain. These results suggest that explicitly training LLMs to self-evolve can lead to more capable and autonomous AI systems.

item.title: Researchers introduce Balance of Benchmarks framework for task-conditioned model comparison using semantic density reweighting and score equating across diverse benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present Balance of Benchmarks (BoB), a framework designed to improve model comparison by adjusting the influence of benchmark scores based on semantic density and task relevance, using only publicly available aggregate scores. BoB addresses limitations of uniform averaging and manual benchmark curation by combining semantic density weighting, score equating across benchmarks of varying difficulty, and task-relevant residual pooling. The framework was evaluated on 605 configurations across 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks and on WildScores, a collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks. BoB-Support improved family-mean Spearman correlation from 0.764 to 0.823, reduced mean absolute error from 6.19 to 5.10 normalized score points, and increased three-model shortlist hit rate from 65.3% to 72.6%. BoB-Constant achieved a Spearman correlation of 0.831 and a hit rate of 74.6%. Additionally, density weighting reduced ranking changes when benchmarks were repeated or paraphrased, and BoB-Support lowered retrospective shortlist regret. The framework makes benchmark inclusion, redundancy, and task relevance explicit and testable, enabling fuller use of existing benchmark evidence while moderating the impact of benchmark proliferation.

item.title: Researchers present LGM, a neuro-symbolic framework for disentangling long-term memory in personalized agents using latent graph construction and query-aware relational weights [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce LGM, a novel neuro-symbolic framework designed to improve personalized agents' reasoning over long-term interaction histories by disentangling memory in a continuous latent space. The approach uses a sparse autoencoder to map historical interactions into latent memory nodes and dynamically synthesizes query-aware relational edge weights, enabling more expressive memory representations. LGM replaces fixed graph structures with tailored latent graphs conditioned on each query, allowing non-linear message passing directed by query embeddings. Experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks show that LGM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in capturing both explicit and implicit user preferences, facilitating more effective personalized responses.

item.title: The Real Cost of AI: A Survey of the Unpredictable Token Economics [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: For decades, enterprise software budgeting was a predictable exercise: negotiate a subscription fee, project the number of seats you need, move on. AI has broken that model. Pricing tied to tokens - the metered unit behind most AI billing - has turned technology spend into a variable cost, and an unpredictable one. The Information's survey of 107 of our readers - senior leaders and professionals (See Methodology) - finds that most companies haven't gotten a handle on it: 60% say the cost trajectory of their AI initiatives is unpredictable, at the exact moment CFOs, boards and investors are demanding proof of ROI. 60%: "The cost trajectory of AI initiatives is unpredictable." This piece draws on that survey and The Information's Deep Research to examine where AI budgets are actually going, why token costs remain so hard to forecast, and what separates the companies that have managed AI spending from those still being surprised by their bills. The Bulk of the AI Budget Outside the hyperscalers, who are pouring billions into data centers, most companies put the bulk of their AI investment - 64% - into software, applications, and API models. (See Chart.) That reflects where ROI is actually realized, according to The Information: most businesses want solutions to specific problems, not infrastructure to manage. This 64% budget line includes the unpredictability factor, the token, which behaves unlike anything else in the technology budget. Let's unpack the costs of different types of software. The classic subscription/SaaS model relies on per-seat licenses for enterprise systems of record and the cloud services that underpin them, such as CRM (Salesforce), ERP/HR and finance (SAP, Workday), and collaboration (Slack). Packaged AI apps and assistants, like ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot, are also largely bought per seat. The flat seat price covers token usage but also limits what an AI assistant can do. The main drawback of seat-based licensing has always been waste: many paid seats sit idle or underused. The token consumption appears in the AI layer of independent digital agents that perform complex tasks rather than simply answering a query. These agents use metered, token-based pricing that scales with usage, making forecasting much harder, and they consume far more compute than basic chatbots. As AI shifts from chatbots to autonomous agents running in the background, the companies least practiced at controlling token usage are seeing the biggest surprises on their bills. That's because such agents operate in loops, and a single inefficient prompt can snowball very quickly. For routine data manipulation and established workflows, traditional software is often still cheaper and more reliable than agentic AI. When budget predictability matters most, AI's consumption-based pricing is a liability, not a feature. One survey respondent frames it as a balancing act: "We should be looking for the best of both worlds. Even with a reasonably implemented, small, hosted cloud environment, the cost per transaction for software is nothing like that of pure agent workloads. The cost of going to pure AI can be prohibitive. There must be a balance among human decisions, programmed software, and pure AI." The Intersection of Token Consumption and Productivity Reader experience with AI productivity varies widely - even within the same industry. One respondent building a startup says, "With my agentic AI assistant, I am compressing what took me 3 years to build into 6 months." A technology lawyer at a large enterprise draws a much tighter line, restricting AI to coding and software-vulnerability remediation. AI is useful for legal research, this reader says, but "the amount of quality control that I have to do with AI-generated content adds to the frustration I feel when having to explain to management why AI can't solve all our problems." Despite the variance, respondents were broadly positive on ROI: 60% say AI increases productivity, more than half say it returns more than it costs, and nearly half report lower internal labor costs. (See Chart) The intersection of "token economics" and workforce productivity has confounded business leaders and accounting departments. First, some companies have equated token consumption with productivity, a mistake. Token consumption itself is not a proxy for a worker's productivity. More tokens don't necessarily mean a better outcome. On the contrary, they can cause AI agents to loop, generating large volumes of responses that can run up compute costs and overwhelm a human. The crux of the issue is translating token consumption into productivity - not equating the two. Token consumption is an input, not an output. It's the compute era's equivalent of billable hours: easy to count, weakly correlated with value. Measure outcomes, not token metrics, with the caveat that outcomes are much harder to measure than tokens. Some metrics that are more useful than tokens to consider include task-completion units (the emerging standard), which count the tasks completed by its agents rather than the tokens processed; cycle-time compression for a given process; and revenue or cost attribution. AI Adoption and Regulatory Compliance "Regulatory compliance is slowing us down" has become one of the most common explanations for sluggish AI adoption. The smallest share of survey respondents, 17%, view regulatory compliance as an accelerant for AI adoption. As government regulations, data privacy laws, and corporate governance requirements increase, the cost to develop, run, and use AI rises significantly. Ensuring that AI acts safely and complies with enterprise parameters requires more "thinking" and therefore more tokens. This is largely because ensuring that models, especially agentic models, are secure, compliant, and safe requires immense computational overhead. While legal uncertainty and the number of regulations are genuine concerns, large companies also face the buildout of AI bureaucracy, including chief AI officers, adoption dashboards, token budgets or governance councils, according to The Information. This bureaucracy is a mechanism to deploy AI at scale but it also obscures whether any of it pays for itself. The economics of AI, especially in the era of tokenization, can be confusing and the AI bureaucracy itself is not its cause but its symptom. Common flaws of AI governance include companies governing AI at the policy layer (committees, principles, training) while risk lives at the identity and permission layer. Most policy frameworks are written as instruction sets delivered to the AI model, while the controls that work (deterministic triggers, permission gates, scoped credentials) are enforced outside the model. On top of that, companies may not always know what they are governing, as vendors and employees are adding shadow AI features. The right approach inverts the framing most companies start with. The default assumption is a tradeoff - compliance slows adoption, so minimize one to maximize the other. The evidence points the other way: the things blocking adoption are the compliance questions, and the companies moving fastest are the ones that resolved them first. But before doing it fast, they must do it right. Token Cost Management Token cost management is where the survey's biggest paradox appears. A slim majority of companies (52%) say they understand token costs, and about as many know that disciplined prompt and output engineering can substantially reduce them. Yet only about a third say they actually control token costs in practice. (See Chart) "Token cost management is not yet in line with the growth in usage of AI," one respondent writes. Only one in five respondents (20%) believe that buying tokens in higher volumes lowers cost-per-query (see Chart). Yet The Information's research shows that batching purchases is an effective and increasingly necessary strategy for cutting per-query costs on frontier models, which carry a steep premium over simpler ones. Equally important for savings is selecting token-guzzling frontier models only for tasks that require them. The Information's research and reader responses point to five ways companies are managing token costs: Train users. Teach employees about model selection, how to prevent models from overthinking, and how to prompt and structure requests to achieve the most useful output at the lowest token cost. Also, teach employees when not to use AI. Match the right model to the right task. Route routine queries to cheaper, open-source models and reserve frontier models for genuinely complex reasoning. "If you select the models best aligned with most tasks, token costs are incredibly low. All the news about token costs concerns frontier models, which are rarely required," one respondent writes. Optimize prompts. Keep them concise, strip unnecessary context, and reuse outputs where possible. The Information's research shows that these "token-minimizing" techniques are being deployed to reduce the volume of data a model must process per request. Cap and track usage. Track token usage against productivity, not just spend, and set daily or weekly caps when usage is outpacing value. At one respondent's company, employees don't have unfettered access to tokens: "Only authorized employees may use tokens, following a defined mandate and an allocated development budget based on a cost-benefit analysis." Adopt a systemic approach. Some respondents argue that the fix isn't behavioral at all. "Cost efficiency is largely determined by systemic, deterministic constraints, rather than individuals voluntarily enforcing constraints upon themselves," one respondent writes. A systemic approach includes creating a single controlled AI gateway (eradicating shadow AI), introducing hard spend ceilings with approval gates, and making the cheapest path automatic. Looking Ahead AI is getting more expensive, not less. The shift from chatbots to autonomous agents built for multi-step workflows is the single biggest driver of rising costs, and token-based pricing means uncontrolled usage shows up directly on the bill. Respondents expect that trend to continue: most see AI-related spending rising across the board over the next 12 months. (See Chart) That's happening as the enterprise AI market moves past its experimental phase and into one where spending gets scrutinized like any other line item. Companies that haven't yet built model routing, usage limits, and hard budget caps into their AI programs are likely to keep absorbing costs they can't fully explain. Methodology Based on a survey of 107 senior leaders and professionals, conducted in June and July 2026. Company size: Forty-five percent of companies surveyed had revenues under $10 million; 20% had revenues of more than $1 billion; 16% had revenues between $10 million and $100 million; 12% had revenues between $100 million and $500 million, and 8% had revenues between $500 million and $1 billion. Key industry sectors: Thirty-eight percent of companies were from technology, media and telecommunications; 13% from professional services; 10% from healthcare and life sciences; 9% from financial services & capital markets, and the remaining 29% came from the government, retail, public sector and others. Respondent titles and roles: Forty percent were executive leadership (including CEOs, CIOs and CTOs) and owners; 31% were senior management (including SVPs and VPs, directors and managers).

item.title: HERMES: Contrast-Aware Knowledge Graph Reasoning from Clinical Notes for Patient Outcome Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical predictive models often rely on structured Electronic Health Record data, such as time-series and procedure codes. While recent approaches have begun leveraging unstructured clinical notes, they typically encode them as flat sequences, which may lose explicit relational and temporal structure present in clinical narratives. In response, we propose HERMES, a graph-based framework that operates exclusively on clinical text while preserving clinical relationships. This approach builds on two key ideas. First, personalized Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are constructed through Large-Language-Model-guided extraction from clinical notes with Contrastive Logic Modeling that explicitly captures temporal dynamics and treatment failures and changes in outcomes. Second, a Graph Attention Network synthesizes patient representations through graph-based learning over the KGs. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV for in-hospital mortality and 30-day readmission prediction show that HERMES consistently outperforms strong text-only baselines. Our findings demonstrate that explicit relational modeling with Contrastive Logic Modeling significantly advances predictive performance.

item.title: TALON: A Temporally Aware Longitudinal Framework for Radiology Report Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current radiology report generation (RRG) models usually produce descriptive reports based on a single examination or only the most recent prior examination, limiting their ability to perform accurate and meaningful longitudinal comparisons and detect subtle interval changes. Although recent approaches have begun to incorporate multiple prior examinations, they usually aggregate a fixed-length history without explicitly modeling the role-dependent relevance of each prior examination before fusion. To address this, we propose TALON, a Temporally Aware LONgitudinal RRG framework that adaptively integrates variable-length patient histories. The underlying Dual-Channel Temporal Fusion Module (DCTFM) compares the current examination with each prior examination through complementary similarity and change channels to capture persistent findings and interval changes, respectively. The specially designed channel-specific attention estimates the relevance of each prior examination, while a learned prior-specific gate adaptively integrates informative longitudinal evidence and suppresses redundancy. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR show that TALON outperforms the current state-of-the-art method on various clinical efficacy and graph-based metrics. When more prior examinations become available, TALON's performance on these metrics improves even further, emphasizing the strength of TALON's DCTFM in modeling longitudinal RRG across longer and more complex patient histories than existing approaches.

item.title: Beyond WER: Entity and Disfluency Recall in Accented Conversational ASR [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ASR systems optimised for Word Error Rate (WER) often miss named entities and filled pauses in accented conversational English, both critical for language-learning feedback. We present a three-stage pipeline for speakers from India, Indonesia, and Latin America: (1) heuristic SQL filters curating entity-rich training data at 2.8x the entity density of random sampling, (2) regional LoRA adapters fine-tuned on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B producing both verbatim and corrected transcripts in a single forward pass, and (3) a six-category error taxonomy validated by an LLM-based judge (83.8% agreement, 210 human-labelled samples). The pipeline achieves 80-85% entity recall (up from 53-55%), 76-86% filler recall (up from <5%), and 6-10% WER across 6k test utterances, outperforming Whisper and a commercial ASR on entity recall while matching a zero-shot 30B model with 10x fewer parameters. Paired bootstrap tests confirm that curation alone accounts for 2.8-4.2 pp of entity recall gain (p<0.0001).

item.title: Recursive Language Models Generalize Out of Domain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study when limiting what a language model can see improves learning. We compare standard CoT, the more general learner that reads the full trace, with recursive language models, which restricts itself by solving each subtask in an isolated context. In-distribution, this generality comes for free: CoT can efficiently simulate the recursive rule, so the IID generalization guarantee changes only by a constant factor, and recursion does not offer much. But out of domain, CoT can fit training by relying on context outside the current subtask, i.e. a shortcut that breaks once those tokens change; recursive context isolation rules out this failure mode. Even though CoT's class still covers the recursive rule, simplicity bias picks the shortcut over the truth. Thus, to go beyond distributional accuracy and truly reason, covering the right rule is not enough; this contrasts with classical learning theory.

item.title: PhysioBench: A Unified Benchmark for Physiological Signal Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physiological signals support diverse clinical and monitoring tasks, yet existing physiological signal foundation models typically require task-specific adaptation for each task. Natural language provides a common interface for specifying different prediction objectives, but the ability of current models to follow such instructions across physiological signal modalities remains insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce PhysioBench, a unified benchmark for physiological signal question answering. PhysioBench harmonizes annotations from 22 public datasets into 61.4 million questions across 30 tasks. Each question-answer pair is grounded in a signal segment and traceable to its source annotation. We evaluate 21 representative models, including large language models, vision-language models, time-series language models, and physiological signal foundation models under three complementary settings. The results show that none of the evaluated models achieves consistently strong performance across physiological signal modalities and tasks. The incorporation of natural language supports unified prediction across tasks, although performance remains sensitive to question formulation. Beyond these findings, PhysioBench offers an extensible platform for fine-grained analysis and future research on physiological signal understanding. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Leanna97/PhysioBench.

item.title: VISPATH: Visual-Intent-Guided Path Reasoning for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) enables models to answer natural-language questions through structured graph reasoning and has achieved substantial progress across many benchmarks and applications. Recently, multimodal KGQA (MM-KGQA) has attracted increasing attention because many questions require jointly using multimodal inputs and KG evidence. However, existing MM-KGQA methods typically use multimodal information only for starting entity grounding or evidence retrieval, after which multi-hop reasoning degenerates into text-only graph search. As a result, they cannot exploit multimodal cues that become important at intermediate hops. To address this limitation, we propose VISPATH, a visual-intent-guided path reasoning framework for MM-KGQA. VISPATH first identifies a reliable starting entity by combining multimodal grounding with graph-structural cues. It then performs intent-guided path discovery by recomputing hop-specific multimodal intent from the input, question, and current partial paths, so that each expansion is guided by the current reasoning state. The discovered paths are further refined through reasoning-chain pruning, which evaluates candidate paths as complete evidence chains based on their consistency with the question, reasoning sketch, and hop-specific intent. Finally, VISPATH checks whether the selected evidence is sufficient for answer generation. We further construct VISPATH-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal multi-hop reasoning over KGs, covering questions that require two to four hops over KG paths. Extensive experiments on VISPATH-Bench and three additional multimodal QA benchmarks show that VISPATH consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, with GPT-4o as the backbone, VISPATH surpasses GPT-5.4 on VISPATH-Bench, achieving a 10.6% relative improvement in average accuracy and a 13.1% improvement at 2-hop reasoning.

item.title: Reading Less While Writing: A Closed-Form Bandwidth Dial for Streaming Multimodal Decoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A decoder that turns video or audio into text conventionally consumes the entire input before emitting a word. Offline this is merely more than the task requires; live it is impossible, since a caption cannot wait for a match to end. Streaming systems bolt on a fixed rule such as wait-$k$, which waits for the same number of input tokens before every word, regardless of the input's length or pace. We replace the fixed offset with ZENDAYA, a schedule governed by a single continuous parameter $\gamma$. It makes the visible source prefix a closed-form function of generation progress, scaled by the input's own predicted length, so an ordinary offline decoder and a real-time streaming decoder become two endpoints of one family rather than separate models. The same scalar fixes, in closed form, the mean fraction of source consumed per emitted word, $\bar{E}(\gamma) \approx 1/(1+\gamma)$, making it at once a latency dial and an interpretable budget. We prove a structural dependency theorem: under any schedule fixed in advance and non-decreasing, no emitted token can depend on input that has not yet arrived. The guarantee holds for trained and untrained weights alike, and extends to unbounded streams under arbitrary asynchronous arrival. The empirical result is counterintuitive: seeing less can produce better text, because a flood of source dilutes attention exactly when the model has the least of its own output to anchor on. Trained from scratch across two modalities and three public corpora (Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, LibriHeavy), a compact 29M-parameter decoder matches or beats the fixed schedule while reading less of the source, with the sharpest gains at the lowest latencies, where a fixed offset collapses. Streaming METEOR gains are statistically significant on all three corpora.

item.title: Rewarding Efficient Reasoning Improves Abstention on Underspecified Tasks in Reasoning Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.20846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While modern large reasoning models (LRMs) excel at providing correct answers in many tasks, we provide additional evidence for the observation that they often struggle with a critical capability: knowing when to abstain from answering. We analyze this gap by comparing LRM behavior to results from a human study, revealing that human reasoning effort on unanswerable tasks is upper-bounded by answerable tasks, whereas LRMs waste computational resources by generating longer Chains of Thought (CoTs) on unanswerable than on answerable prompts. To overcome this inefficiency, we take inspiration from a resource-rational perspective on human cognition and introduce a novel GRPO reward that encourages efficient reasoning about whether the task contains all the information needed to solve it. Fine-tuning several 4B LRMs with this reward leads to human-like abstention performance gains (+12.8% on average) while retaining answering capabilities and boosting the models' efficiency (44% shorter CoTs on average).

item.title: Aligning with Lived Experience: Heterogeneous Benefits of Fine Tuning in Mental Health Support Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As access to professional mental healthcare remains limited, many individuals turn to online platforms such as Reddit to seek peer support situated within human lived experience. However, a significant portion of such queries go unanswered, presenting an opportunity for using Large Language Models (LLMs) to fill this gap. While LLMs have demonstrated strong performance on clinical benchmarks, their ability to generate lived-experience informed and community-aligned peer support is underexplored. Addressing this gap, we introduce the COmmunity-centered Peer Engaged Support (COPES) dataset and a three-axis evaluation framework to assess LLM alignment with community perspectives to mental health support seeking queries. Evaluating zero-shot and post-trained (SFT and DPO) models, we show that post-training on COPES significantly improves Strategy Alignment (>50% for general-purpose models) and alignment in Emotion & Tone. However, we also observe that such improvements are heterogeneous and alignment improvements vary significantly across subreddits and requested coping strategies. Furthermore, post-training induces distributional shifts, heavily favoring problem-focused recommendations while suppressing emotion-focused strategies. Together, this work shows that while curating community-driven data improves the alignment of LLM responses, model performance remains disparate across distinct sub-communities and specific mental health needs.

item.title: Geometry of Values: Task Vector Composition for Ethical Preference Alignment in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in applications that must weigh clashing moral values, yet even strong models exhibit hidden biases and brittle instruction-following across languages. We introduce a 12,000-instance dataset of two-option dilemmas covering pairwise three value conflicts: Honesty vs. Justice, Justice vs. Autonomy, and Autonomy vs. Honesty, along with their translations into Hindi, Arabic, Spanish, and Chinese, to probe cross-lingual behavior. Benchmarking on GPT-5-mini reveals that it consistently favors Honesty over Autonomy across all five languages when no policy is given. The Llama-3.2-1/3B models exhibit strong first-option bias; however, both plain fine-tuning and Direct Preference Optimization fine-tuning effectively remove this bias, increasing accuracy to greater than 98%. In order to decouple the effect of learning correlations in the dataset from abstract values, we propose a task vector transfer based experiment where after computing the task vectors for a direction of value preference we orthogonalize it with respect to the general instruction following vector. Our experiment shows that this method is effective in isolating the direction of the specific value preference that can successfully be used to conduct task arithmetic to obtain a model with the opposite stance.

item.title: From Task Success to Productive Success: Evaluating Human-AI Collaboration by Quality and Cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI productivity is often measured by task completion time, economic value, or improvements in outcome quality. However, these measures usually treat collaboration as a black box where they capture what output was produced, but not the interaction cost required to produce it. Motivated by economics literature, we introduce a productivity-oriented framework for evaluating human-AI collaboration as outcome quality relative to interaction cost. Across two datasets spanning four tasks, we show that: (1) sessions with identical quality ratings can differ by up to 70 times in interaction cost; (2) quality-cost relationships vary by task, with some tasks rewarding extended interaction and others favoring fast convergence; (3) subjective user ratings are not reliable substitutes for productivity; and (4) productive sessions are characterized by agents probing earlier and users spending less effort repairing the interaction. By distinguishing productive success from costly success, our framework makes interactional cost visible and shows how dialogue analysis can inform the evaluation and design of AI systems.

item.title: Hallucination-R1: Robustness-Oriented Paraphrase Generation for Factual Consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Factual hallucination is commonly defined by incorrect factual outputs. We study a paraphrase-induced hallucination setting, where a model answers a factual question correctly in its original form but generates an incorrect answer under a semantically equivalent paraphrase. Such inconsistencies expose latent factual instability under semantic invariance. However, general-purpose paraphrases are often insufficient as robustness-oriented supervision: near-copy paraphrases provide weak signals, while overly diverse paraphrases may break semantic equivalence. In this paper, we propose HALLUCINATION-R1, a robustness-oriented paraphrase generation framework that learns to produce semantically faithful yet robustness-challenging paraphrases for factual consistency. Through two-stage optimization, it first stabilizes meaning-preserving and diverse paraphrasing, then rewards paraphrases that reveal factual consistency degradation in downstream QA models. Experiments on SimpleQuestions, PopQA, and TruthfulQA show that HALLUCINATION-R1 achieves a strong consistency--diversity trade-off and exposes robustness failures across multiple model families and datasets. Further analyses indicate that these failures are not reducible to surface-level artifacts or semantic drift, but reveal non-trivial factual instability under meaning-preserving variation. A lightweight fine-tuning study also shows that HALLUCINATION-R1-generated data improves robust accuracy under paraphrase variations, suggesting its utility for robustness-oriented training. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/yuwenhan07/Hallucination-R1.

item.title: How Many Humans Is a Judge Panel Worth? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How many human judgments does a panel of language models represent? The answer depends on what is matched. We audit categorical judge panels against empirical human label distributions, retaining disagreement that binary errors relative to one gold label collapse. We measure spectral residual diversity by matching the participation ratio of a normalized residual Gram matrix to conditionally independent human-reference draws, giving nu_H. We separately match distributional squared error, giving nu_MSE. Across three ChaosNLI tasks, the same 32-judge panels have nu_H=4.24--6.50 but nu_MSE=2.30--3.75. A spectral identity separates the eigenvalues, member energies, and averaging-direction weights that determine error. Realizable hard-label panels show that greater spectral diversity can accompany worse distribution recovery even with equal member energies and nonnegative correlations. In the observed panels, within-size ranking agreement varies sharply by task; some member additions produce conflicting changes that persist across two item halves. The consensus-direction share of centered residual variance is gamma_co=43.8% on MNLI-m and 33.7% on SNLI, quantifying shared variation retained by averaging. We provide aligned votes and analysis protocols for auditing these distinctions. Effective size is therefore a target-specific measurement: spectral diversity and distribution recovery should not be treated as interchangeable measures of panel quality or as general human-replacement rates.

item.title: From Memory to Behavior: A Behavior-Aware Role-Playing Framework for Social Media Influencers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have shown strong potential as role-playing agents for real individuals, yet faithful impersonating remains challenging. Existing in-context learning-based methods fail to capture how individuals react under different situations. In addition, LLM-based evaluation is difficult for obscure individuals. To address these challenges, we propose Situation--Internal state--Behavior Persona method to incorporate situation-dependent behavioral strategies. We further design an evaluation protocol that provides LLM evaluators with references about the impersonated individual. We evaluate our approach on a newly constructed dataset for the task of generating replies on social media. Experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art ICL-based baselines, while our evaluation protocol achieves moderate correlation with human judgment. Besides, experiments on fictional-character benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method is applicable beyond the social media setting. These findings suggest that incorporating behavioral information broadly improves the fidelity of role-playing for real individuals on social media or fictional characters.

item.title: Prediction Dynamics in Depth-Recurrent Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.21383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Depth-recurrent language models refine predictions through repeated latent updates. Why can intermediate answers agree with the endpoint while their scores continue to change? We derive a sharp margin characterization that decomposes the conservatism of a magnitude bound into common translation, direction relative to the winner, and the pairing of each competitor's update with its score gap. Across Huginn-3.5B and Ouro-1.4B, accounting for update direction and competitor pairing reduces the mean earliest qualifying depth by a further 22.5-34.4% of the total depth beyond translation removal under full answer-text scoring. This retrospective comparison uses completed trajectories. Substantial contributions also occur under label scoring. For shared predictive distributions, we separate common and contrast motion orthogonally and express the common component through candidate-set mass and within-set concentration. Common and contrast energies can attenuate at different rates, allowing a growing preference-change share to coexist with shrinking absolute updates. These findings explain finite-depth answer preservation through the geometry and composition of observed score changes.

item.title: Consistent Relexicalization of Clinical Documents using Graph-Based Approach [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
